summary: Extends the Session Description Protocol (SDP) with capability negotiation parameters and offer/answer procedures, in a backward compatible way. It allows negotiating alternative transport protocols and attributes, such as Secure RTP or different keying methods. It is a Proposed Standard.

plainLanguage.summary: Two people pick a language to talk in. This lets the devices list what they can do and agree on the best way to talk.

questions: how to negotiate srtp in sdp
what does a=pcfg mean in sdp
subtitle: How an SDP offer can list alternative transports and attributes, such as plain RTP or Secure RTP, and let the other side pick.

tldr.problem: SDP and the offer/answer model have no way to offer alternative transport protocols or attributes, which makes it hard to deploy new RTP profiles such as Secure RTP.
tldr.mechanism: The offer carries capabilities (a=tcap, a=acap) and potential configurations (a=pcfg) as ordinary SDP attributes. The answer reports the chosen one in a=acfg.
tldr.outcome: Endpoints that do not know the framework ignore the new attributes and fall back to plain RFC 3264 behaviour. RFC 6871 later updated this RFC.

facts.label: New attributes
facts.value: 6: csup, creq, acap, tcap, pcfg, acfg

today: RFC 5939 is a Proposed Standard and has been updated by RFC 6871. It remains the base specification of the SDP capability negotiation framework described here.

sections.title: The Problem with Plain SDP
sections.content:
The Session Description Protocol (SDP) was meant to describe multimedia sessions. The offer/answer model of RFC 3264 let two parties agree on a session: the offerer lists streams, codecs and parameters, and the answerer picks from them. But SDP does not say how to negotiate alternative transport protocols (for example RTP profiles) or attributes.

That makes new profiles hard to deploy. The RFC points out that supporting plain and Secure RTP, each with and without RTCP-based feedback, takes four separate profiles: RTP/AVP, RTP/SAVP, RTP/AVPF and RTP/SAVPF. Keying material is also needed for some transports but not others.

The RFC is explicit about its limits. It does not aim to be a full capability protocol like SDPng or ITU-T H.245. It targets a set of well-known real-life limitations and stays backwards compatible with existing SDP. Attributes and transport protocols are defined as capabilities; other kinds, such as media types and formats, are left to other documents.
sections.plainLanguage: Plain SDP is like inviting someone to one exact kind of game. If they only know a different game, the invitation fails. This RFC lets you say which other games you could also play.

sections.title: Capabilities and Configurations
sections.content:
The RFC splits the problem into four ideas. Capabilities are what a side supports, such as the RTP/SAVP profile or a crypto attribute with a given value; listing one is not a commitment to use it. Potential configurations say which combinations of capabilities could be used, subject to further negotiation. An actual configuration can be used right away. The negotiation process takes actual and potential configurations in and produces the negotiated actual configurations.

Plain SDP only expresses the actual configuration. Conceptually, the offerer sends the actual configuration plus alternatives, and the answerer picks one and says which. In practice everything fits in one SDP description using new attributes. Because receivers ignore unknown attributes, an entity without support simply does the normal RFC 3264 exchange. Encoding capabilities compactly also keeps messages small when there are many combinations.
sections.plainLanguage: A capability is a list of toys you own. A potential configuration is a short list of toy combinations you would like to play with. The actual configuration is the toy already on the table.

sections.title: The Six New Attributes
sections.content:
The solution adds six SDP attributes. Two describe the framework itself: a=csup lists supported extension option tags and a=creq lists extensions the receiver must support. Two express capabilities: a=acap for an attribute and its value, and a=tcap for transport protocols. Two negotiate: a=pcfg lists potential configurations by reference to capabilities, and a=acfg in the answer names the potential configuration that was used.

By default, potential configurations are preferred over the actual configuration in the m= line. That lets an offerer who wants Secure RTP but can live with plain RTP put plain RTP in the actual configuration and Secure RTP in a potential configuration. Entities that do not understand the framework default to plain RTP.

In the RFC's example, Alice offers plain RTP with a Secure RTP alternative, and Bob picks Secure RTP and says so with a=acfg. Alice then sends a second offer that uses SRTP as the actual configuration, purely to help intermediaries that do not understand the framework.
sections.plainLanguage: You write your usual plan on the front of a card and your favourite plan on the back. If your friend can read the back they use it, and they tell you they did. If not, they just follow the front.

sections.title: Attribute Syntax and Rules
sections.content:
a=acap:<num> <attribute> and a=tcap:<num> <proto-list> give each capability a number between 1 and 2^31-1. Each number must be unique in its own namespace across the whole description. A capability must not embed other capability negotiation attributes, which avoids recursive processing. A transport protocol must be listed in a tcap even if it appears in the m= line, so that an intermediary that rewrites the line cannot invalidate the reference.

a=pcfg:<config-number> ... appears only at the media level. A lower configuration number is preferred. It may hold a transport list such as t=4|3, where alternatives are separated by a vertical bar in order of preference, and an attribute list such as a=-m:1,2,[3,4]. Square brackets mark optional attribute capabilities, and a leading -m, -s or -ms deletes the existing media-level, session-level or both sets of attributes. An omitted list means the potential configuration equals the actual one.

a=csup carries comma-separated option tags, and the base tag is cap-v0. A recipient that cannot support a tag in a=creq must skip capability negotiation and proceed as if the attributes were absent.
sections.plainLanguage: Each option gets a number, like numbered seats. The plan says "use seat 1 for the transport and seat 2 for the lock", and a lower plan number means "I like this one more".

sections.title: Offer and Answer Procedures
sections.content:
The offerer includes any capabilities and, in each media description where it wants alternatives, one or more a=pcfg attributes. Capabilities alone are not a commitment; each potential configuration is an alternative offer the offerer would like used. The offerer must not reference a media-level capability from another media description.

The answerer works on each media description separately. It discards invalid potential configurations, then tries the valid ones from the lowest configuration number up. Conceptually it builds an internal offer: a chosen transport replaces the one in the m= line, and chosen attribute capabilities are added before the existing attributes. All mandatory capabilities must be supported. If none works, the answerer uses the actual configuration. The answer carries a=acfg with the chosen configuration number and the parameters actually used. a=creq must not appear in an answer.

The offerer reads a=acfg and processes the answer as if the offer had been the chosen potential configuration. If a potential configuration was chosen and differs from the actual one, the offerer SHOULD start a second offer/answer exchange with it as the actual configuration, so non-aware intermediaries see what was negotiated.
sections.plainLanguage: The friend checks your choices from your favourite down. They use the first one they can do, then tell you the number of the one they used.

sections.title: Practical Concerns
sections.content:
The offerer must be ready to receive media for the actual configuration, but media sent under a potential configuration may be discarded until the answer arrives, causing clipping. The RFC therefore recommends answering as soon as possible. A three-way handshake, using SIP preconditions or an ICE STUN binding request, can avoid the problem.

Bandwidth is not negotiated by the base framework, so the b= value should cover the worst case across potential configurations. It is also easy to create offers with many potential configurations, and the RFC recommends against unnecessarily large numbers. Answerers must guard memory and CPU, for example by first discarding configurations with unsupported transports or mandatory capabilities.

Intermediaries that do not support the framework, such as session border controllers, may reject an answer with a different transport, or authorize resources based on the wrong configuration. The RFC recommends that intermediary implementers add support.
sections.plainLanguage: If your friend starts talking before they have told you which language they picked, you might miss the start. So they should tell you quickly. Too many choices also tire the friend out, so keep the list short.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Offering alternatives with different strengths means an attacker who can change the offer could force the weakest option the offerer is willing to accept, including plain RTP if it was offered as a fallback. The RFC's remedy is integrity protection of the SDP, ideally end-to-end (for example S/MIME), or SIP Identity, or weaker hop-by-hop protection such as TLS or IPsec.

Another issue is that the offerer must accept media for the actual configuration before the answer arrives, so an attacker might send media in that window. Ways to reduce this include not offering the non-secure stream as the actual configuration, using SDP security preconditions, or answering quickly. Modifying or removing a=acfg can cause failure. Finally, a large offer can be used for denial of service against the answerer.
sections.plainLanguage: If a trickster can edit your note, they might cross out the safe options and leave only the unsafe one. Sealing the note so nobody can change it solves that.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content: IANA registered the six new SDP attributes: csup, creq, acap, tcap, pcfg and acfg. It also created two registries: one for capability negotiation option tags and one for potential configuration parameters. Both require an RFC under the IETF Review policy. The option tag cap-v0 and the parameters a (attribute) and t (transport protocol) are registered by this document.
sections.plainLanguage: The new words were written in an official dictionary, and a rulebook says how anyone can add more.
